newsitem.title: USA: Florida judge's ruling strengthens tobacco's defense.
newsitem.headline: Florida judge's ruling strengthens tobacco's defense.

text.p: A Florida judge presiding over the state's $1 billion lawsuit against the tobacco industry said on Friday that cigarette makers will be allowed to present evidence that their advertising did not mislead the public about the dangers of smoking.

Palm Beach Circuit Judge Harold Cohen also said the tobacco companies may introduce documents or direct testimony from corporate executives to show there never was any intent to mislead anyone about the hazards of smoking.
"I am going to allow relevent evidence that the defendants believe (showed) the public was aware of the risks of smoking because the information was in the public domain," he ruled.

However, Cohen made it clear that the only documents the tobacco companies could use to rebut the state's charges of fraudulent advertising and racketeering were those that company officials relied on in making their decision.

The ruling pertained only with the racketeering and fraud counts of Florida's landmark lawsuit against the industry, which seeks to recover the costs of treating Medicaid recipients with smoking-related illnesses.
It did not affect a prior ruling by Cohen, in which he said the industry could not use public knowledge about the dangers of smoking as a defense against the state's Medicaid allegations.

In that ruling, Cohen said the only defenses the tobacco companies could use were that their cigarettes were not defective, that they did not cause the harm claimed by the defendants and consequently were not responsible for the expense the state incurred in caring for Medicaid patients.
David Bernick, who represents the British American Tobacco Co., said defense attorneys were "grateful that the court recognized ... we had the right to demonstrate that we had no criminal intent."
Michael Maher, one of Florida's attorneys, said the ruling was "a strong decision in the state's favor" because it could bring tobacco company executives to the witness stand.
"It forces the defendants to bring their executives who made the decision to court to explain why and how they made their decisions," he said.

Attorneys for the two sides will begin individual questioning of jury candidates on Monday. During two weeks of pre-screening, Cohen winnowed a jury pool of more than 300 to 124, from which six jurors and nine alternates will be chosen.
Opening arguments are expected to take place soon after Labor Day with the trial lasting until January.
Cohen also said he would hold a hearing before the end of August on whether Florida could use any of the widely published Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. documents at trial.

The tobacco companies claim the documents were stolen and cannot be used. If the documents were stolen, Cohen said, they may not be used during the trial any more than attorneys could use evidence obtained illegally in a criminal trial.
"We look forward to showing just how these document were obtained," said Stephen Kriegbaum, a Philip Morris attorney.
J. Anderson Berly, one of Florida's attorneys, said the documents may have been originally stolen but Florida obtained them legally through a court order in a Mississppi case.
